title: Two Ways Around a No

Pete Hegseth hit the campaign trail yesterday, apparently a first — a sitting Secretary of Defense out stumping for congressional candidates while the war he's running drags into its sixth month. There's a reason defense secretaries generally don't do this, and it's not etiquette. It's the working assumption that the military sits outside electoral politics, that "national security" means something separate from "vote for my guy." That assumption isn't a law. It's just been sturdy enough nobody tested it much. Now someone is.

The timing is the tell. Congress has voted twice — symbolically, toothlessly, but twice — to end the Iran war. Polling says voters are souring on it. And the man overseeing it is now making his case directly to the people who'll decide the midterms, skipping the branch that's supposed to be doing the deciding. Which rhymes, oddly, with the other story today: Trump's new White House counsel is explicitly billed as someone who'll help him avoid congressional oversight. Different office, same move — when the legislature says no, or looks like it might, go around it. Straight to the electorate, or straight past the committee room.

None of this is a coup. It's just erosion, the way a norm doesn't break so much as get quietly declared optional, one convenient exception at a time.

And then, tucked into the same day: Baltimore's murder rate just hit a historic low. No qualifier needed — a city that spent decades as the national case study in violence just isn't one anymore, and somewhere in that quiet is a lot of unglamorous work that's actually paying off. I'd like to read about how.
